Newborn Care

The sucking reflex and your baby’s feeding skills

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited byMohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Babies arrive with automatic responses that help them adapt to life outside the womb. Sucking is one of these reflexes, but feeding also requires swallowing, breathing and enough energy to keep going. Knowing what to observe (and when to ask for help) can make those early feeds less uncertain.

Sucking begins automatically, but feeding is a coordinated skill

A reflex is a response that happens without a baby deciding to make it. A newborn may begin to suck when a nipple or teat stimulates the mouth. This response helps with feeding, but it is only one part of the task: milk also has to be swallowed while the baby continues to breathe comfortably.

A baby can have a noticeable sucking reflex and still struggle to transfer enough milk. Strength, alertness, positioning, milk flow, illness and endurance all influence a feed. Watching the whole feeding pattern is more useful than judging one movement or the number of minutes spent at the breast.

Development starts before birth and continues afterward

Sucking movements can be seen before birth, sometimes during an ultrasound when a baby brings a hand to the mouth. The response becomes more organised in the third trimester. Descriptions of development around 32 to 36 weeks should not be read as a precise start date for every sucking movement or a guarantee of feeding readiness.

Coordination of sucking, swallowing and breathing generally develops around 34 to 36 weeks of pregnancy, but individual babies vary. A baby born earlier may have an immature pattern or tire before finishing a feed. A full-term baby can also need help, particularly if sleepy, unwell or having difficulty with attachment.

Premature babies may need a bridge to oral feeding

A neonatal team assesses readiness rather than relying only on gestational age. Breast milk or another prescribed feed may initially be given through a tube entering the nose or mouth and passing into the stomach. This provides nutrition while the baby develops skills or recovers from illness. It is not evidence that a parent has failed.

Some babies combine tube feeding with gradually increasing breast or bottle feeds. Respiratory support, breathing stability and fatigue affect the plan. Sucking on a dummy, also called a pacifier, uses a different pattern from drinking milk, so a strong non-feeding suck is not permission to increase oral feeds or remove a feeding tube without the team.

How the mouth moves milk during a feed

At the breast, the baby takes a mouthful of breast tissue as well as the nipple and forms a seal. Coordinated tongue and jaw movements, together with pressure changes in the mouth, draw milk from the breast. The tongue helps manage the milk and move it toward a swallow. The action is sometimes described as expression followed by a milking movement, although real feeding is a continuous coordinated process.

A bottle-fed baby also needs a seal, effective sucking, controlled milk flow and time to breathe. A faster teat is not necessarily easier for a baby with immature coordination. Signs of stress, repeated coughing, gulping or difficulty keeping up with the flow warrant a feeding assessment and an individual plan.

Rooting helps a baby find the breast or teat

Rooting and sucking work together but do different jobs. Touch near the cheek or corner of the mouth can prompt a baby to turn and open the mouth toward it. This helps locate the nipple; sucking then helps move milk once the breast or teat is in the mouth.

Early searching movements may be broad and become more directed with experience. Rooting often becomes less obvious by about four months as feeding becomes more purposeful. Hand-to-mouth movements and rooting can be early feeding cues, but older babies also suck their hands for comfort or exploration. One cue alone does not tell you how much milk they have had.

Observe feeding instead of repeatedly testing reflexes

A clinician may assess sucking with a clean or gloved finger or observe the baby at the breast or bottle. At home, there is no need to press on the roof of the mouth, repeatedly insert objects or try to provoke a response. A sleepy or distressed baby may respond differently, and a home test cannot diagnose a neurological or swallowing problem.

Ask for a feed to be observed if sucking seems consistently weak, feeds are exhausting, the baby repeatedly loses the latch or you are worried about milk transfer. A feeding professional can assess mouth movements, position, swallowing, breathing and stamina together. A reduced reflex that becomes a more controlled skill is different from a real loss of feeding ability, which needs review.

Use intake and wellbeing signs to judge progress

Look for swallowing during feeds, periods of comfortable sucking, wet nappies and an appropriate weight trend. In the early days, nappy output changes quickly; by around day five, at least six heavy wet nappies in 24 hours is a useful general sign for a breastfed newborn. Weight checks and the baby’s overall condition remain important, rather than treating a nappy number as a guarantee.

Seek prompt advice if feeding is poor, urine is less than expected, jaundice is increasing or your baby is unusually sleepy. Repeated choking, distress, wet or gurgly breathing around feeds, or poor growth also needs assessment. Some swallowing problems do not cause obvious coughing. If a baby cannot breathe, becomes blue or grey, goes limp or is unresponsive, stop the feed and call emergency services.

Offer skin-to-skin care safely

Close skin-to-skin contact can support warmth, comfort and opportunities to feed. Keep the face visible, the airway clear and the head and body supported. The adult needs to be awake and able to watch the baby. Ask for help with positioning after pain medicine, surgery or when either of you has medical needs.

Kangaroo mother care combines prolonged skin-to-skin contact with support for breast-milk feeding and is recommended for preterm or low-birth-weight babies. It can begin early with appropriate clinical support; it is not restricted to a few unusual diagnoses. Babies needing intensive treatment require a team plan for safe care. Skin-to-skin contact does not replace a cot and a safe sleep arrangement when the caregiver is going to sleep.

Follow feeding cues and any prescribed waking schedule

Breastfed newborns commonly feed about eight to twelve times in 24 hours. Spacing varies, and some feeds cluster close together. A sleepy baby may need waking to meet nutritional needs, particularly with prematurity, jaundice or concerns about weight. Follow the schedule given by the maternity or neonatal team instead of assuming every baby can safely wait until they wake.

Gentle stroking, a nappy change or adjusting clothing can help rouse a sleepy baby. Never shake a baby to wake them. If the baby cannot be woken enough to feed, seek prompt medical help. There is no universal age when waking should stop; the decision depends on effective feeding, weight progress and health.

Adjust position and milk flow with support

Try a comfortable position with the baby’s head and body aligned and close to you. A cross-cradle or underarm hold may make support easier; a pillow or rolled towel can support your arm while you remain awake and attentive. Avoid forcing the back of the baby’s head. At the breast, waiting for a wide mouth and bringing the baby close can help achieve a deeper attachment.

If milk is slow to flow, a feeding professional may suggest brief warmth, gentle handling or a little hand expression before the feed. Avoid painful or forceful breast massage and overheating. If milk flow is overwhelming, a change of position or a different plan may be more helpful than trying to increase it.

For bottle feeds, hold and support the baby, allow pauses and respond to stress or fullness cues. Do not prop the bottle or force it to be finished. A clinician can advise on teat flow and positioning when coordination is difficult. A longer feed is not automatically a better feed; repeated exhaustion is a reason to review the plan.

Use feeding aids and tube-feeding experiences thoughtfully

A lactation consultant, midwife, nurse or clinician can help with attachment, expressing, milk supply and breast or nipple pain. Some babies need a nipple shield or another aid, but its fit, effect on milk transfer and ongoing need should be reviewed. An aid should come with instructions and follow-up, rather than replacing an assessment of why feeding is difficult.

If your baby is tube fed, ask the neonatal team about holding, skin-to-skin care and appropriate non-nutritive sucking experiences. Do not place loose cotton wool soaked in milk near the nose or mouth, or introduce milk through an unapproved route. The aim is a safe, pleasant experience that fits the baby’s readiness. Improvement may take time and specialist input; practice alone does not solve every feeding problem.

Moro and tonic neck responses change in early infancy

The Moro response is a startle-like movement: a baby may extend the limbs after a sudden sensation or noise and then draw them back in, sometimes crying. It is prominent early in life and starts to fade over the first few months. Descriptions of the age at which it disappears vary, so a single age is not a home deadline. Do not drop the baby’s head or make loud noises to demonstrate it.

If swaddling helps settle your baby, follow safe-sleep advice: place them on their back, avoid overheating or tight wrapping around the hips, and stop swaddling when they show signs of rolling. Swaddling is optional and does not treat a neurological problem.

With the asymmetric tonic neck response, turning the head may be accompanied by extension of the arm on that side and bending of the opposite arm, sometimes called a fencing posture. It can be subtle and usually becomes less evident by about five to seven months. Do not force the neck to test it. Report persistent movement differences between the two sides.

Grasp, Babinski and stepping are different responses

Touching the palm can cause the fingers to close around an object. This palmar grasp develops before birth and is usually present in a newborn, becoming less reflexive around five to six months. Never lift a baby by their grip: an automatic grasp can release without warning, however strong it feels.

The Babinski response involves the big toe moving upward and the other toes spreading when the sole is stimulated. It can be normal in infancy and may remain present up to about two years. It is different from the plantar grasp, in which the toes curl. Interpretation belongs to a clinical examination; parents do not need to repeatedly stroke or press the foot to obtain a result.

A supported newborn may make stepping movements when the soles contact a surface. The early stepping reflex usually fades around two months. It does not mean the baby can stand independently or is ready to practise walking. Keep full head and body support during handling and allow later movement skills to develop at their own pace.

Use developmental ages as context, not a pass-or-fail chart

As a broad guide, rooting often becomes less obvious around four months, palmar grasp around five to six months and tonic neck responses around five to seven months; early stepping tends to fade around two months. Moro responses fade during early infancy, while the Babinski response can remain normal much longer, up to about two years. These are approximate patterns, and prematurity affects interpretation.

Sucking becomes increasingly voluntary and adaptable during infancy; the early reflex becoming less obvious does not mean a baby should lose the ability to drink at four months. Clinicians assess reflexes alongside muscle tone, movement, alertness, feeding and growth. Bring concerns about persistent asymmetry, loss of a skill or poor feeding to the baby’s clinician. Early support is more useful than waiting for a child to meet an exact chart date.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Feeding readiness depends on coordination and health as well as gestational age.

Reflex ages are approximate; intake, growth and a clinical examination provide a fuller picture than home testing.

How BeMama can help

Ask someone experienced to watch a complete feed, including the pauses and signs of tiredness, rather than only checking the latch.

When to seek help

Get prompt help for a baby who feeds poorly or is difficult to wake. Call emergency services for inability to breathe, blue or grey colour, limpness or unresponsiveness.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Rooting finds the nipple; sucking is part of moving milk.
  • A strong suck on a dummy does not prove readiness for full oral feeds.
  • Premature babies may need tube feeding while skills mature.
  • Use nappies, weight, swallowing and wellbeing to assess intake.
  • Do not provoke startles, force neck movements or lift a baby by their grasp.

Frequently asked questions

Does sucking begin exactly at 32 weeks?

No single week describes all sucking movements. Activity begins before birth and becomes more organised later in pregnancy; feeding coordination is a separate milestone.

Can a premature baby with a strong dummy suck safely finish a bottle?

Not necessarily. Drinking adds milk flow, swallowing and breathing demands. The neonatal team should decide how oral feeds progress.

What is the difference between rooting and sucking?

Rooting helps the baby turn toward and locate the nipple. Sucking helps move milk after the breast or teat is in the mouth.

Should I test the reflex with a finger at home?

Repeated home testing is unnecessary and cannot confirm safe swallowing or adequate intake. Ask a clinician to assess a feed if you are concerned.

Will my baby stop feeding when the reflex fades?

No. Feeding becomes more controlled as development continues. An actual loss of feeding ability needs assessment and should not be dismissed as reflex integration.

Must I wake every newborn at exactly three-hour intervals?

Feeding plans vary. Many newborns need frequent feeds and some need waking; follow advice based on weight, jaundice, prematurity and feeding effectiveness.

Is kangaroo care only for a small group of babies?

No. It is recommended for preterm and low-birth-weight babies with appropriate support. The care team helps adapt it to medical needs.

Can I use milk-soaked cotton wool beside a tube-fed baby’s nose?

Do not use loose cotton wool near the nose or mouth. Ask the neonatal team which supervised sensory or sucking experiences are appropriate.

Can I lift my baby if they grip my fingers firmly?

No. A reflex grasp can release suddenly. Always support the head and body securely.

Does a reflex that differs on one side need checking?

Yes. Mention persistent asymmetry or a change in movement to the clinician. A single home observation cannot diagnose the cause, but it is worth reporting.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
